newsitem.title: JAPAN: US warns Japan will fall behind without open skies.
newsitem.headline: US warns Japan will fall behind without open skies.

text.p: The United States warned Japan on Thursday it would be left behind in international aviation markets if it failed to lend a warm ear to U.S. "open skies" proposals.

Other Asian nations would soon begin negotiating open skies accords and it was in Japan's interest to join this movement, Alan Larson, assistant secretary of state for economic and business affairs, told a news conference.
"The world is moving in this direction. Countries that delay or resist risk being left behind," he said, adding that civil aviation was now the most contentious issue between the two economic giants.
His statements come on the eve of "exploratory" talks in Tokyo between officials on whether to resume formal negotiations -- deadlocked since August -- in their long-running air services dispute.

The United States says its open skies proposal would mean the lifting of all government restrictions except for safety and security rules. Resulting competition would bring increased air traffic and lower prices for consumers, said Larson.
"Under open skies, Japanese carriers will be free to establish any service they wish," he said.
He added that Washington would be prepared to accept a phased approach and entertain the possibility of revisions to the current bilateral pact.
But Japan, which believes that the current agreement signed in 1952 favours the United States, is wary.

"This (idea of) open skies will simply invite a domination of international markets by American mega-carriers," Jiro Hanyu, deputy general of the Transport Ministry's civil aviation bureau, told reporters last month.
Hanyu said the United States was calling for open skies without opening it domestic market and urged for a safeguard mechanism to prevent a monopoly by U.S carriers.
"The present situation, under which Japan Airlines cannot fly to such cities as Detroit and Dallas...must be corrected," he said.
The United States has already concluded open skies pacts with 12 European countries, including Germany, and with Jordan.
Larson also criticised Japan for refusing to approve applications for air freight services which Washington believes should be approved under the 1952 agreement.
He said the 1952 agreement was not unfair but that U.S. carriers had simply "out-competed" their Japanese counterparts over the last 15 years.
